home_feat_failure_desc: Narrow down why a part broke from its fracture surface and service
about_failure: answer questions about fracture features and service conditions to see candidate failure modes, how to tell them apart and how to prevent them, plus case studies of accidents caused by material failures.
failure_look: How to recognize it (fracture surface, microstructure, SEM)
failure_score_for: Clues that score for this mode
failure_table_combo: Combination points (added when both are selected)
failure_empty: Answer the questions and the candidate failure modes will be listed here, with the clues behind each one.
failure_n_answered: {n} {n|question|questions} answered. Candidates are listed by points. Points are not probabilities, and the ranking is not a diagnosis.
failure_next: Answering “{q}” next will help separate {a} from {b}.
failure_unlikely: Modes that do not fit your current answers
failure_none_fit: No failure mode has a positive score with these answers. Review your answers or set some back to “Don’t know”.
failure_noscript: Ranking the candidates needs JavaScript. You can still read how to recognize each mode and the scoring table below.
failure_url_note: Your answers are kept in this page’s URL, so the link opens the same answers and candidates. Nothing is sent to a server.
failure_modes_h: How to recognize and prevent each failure mode
failure_modes_lead: The {n} failure modes this guide covers, with how to recognize them, tests to confirm them, common mix-ups and prevention.
failure_cases_lead: Well-known accidents caused by material failures. Facts and figures are limited to those confirmed in official investigation reports and sources that cite them.
failure_table_lead: Candidates are ranked by adding up the points in this table. A plus means the clue fits the mode; a minus means it does not.
failure_case_happened: Sequence of events and the investigation’s findings
failure_case_chain: The chain of causes from the materials side
failure_case_clues: The clues that revealed the cause
failure_open_preset: Open the guide with this case’s clues
failure_case_changes: What changed afterwards: design, rules and inspection
failure_case_sources_note: Dates, numbers of people, dimensions, temperatures and other values were checked against the official reports above and sources that cite them.
failure_back: Back to the failure analysis guide
home_feat_atlas_desc: Compare metal microstructures as schematics; learn to identify them and measure grain size
about_atlas: compare metal microstructures such as ferrite, pearlite, martensite and graphite in cast iron as schematic drawings, with their features, how they form, how they look after etching and how to tell them apart, plus a grain size number converter and an identification quiz.
atlas_noscript: The schematics, grain size converter and quiz need JavaScript. The text can be read without it.
atlas_list_lead: {n} microstructures, grouped by how they form. Tap a drawing to open how to identify it.
atlas_entries_lead: Tap a name to open its schematic, what you see, how it forms and how to tell it from look-alikes.
atlas_frac_hypo: Steel with {c}% C: mass fraction of pearlite by the lever rule {p}%
atlas_frac_hyper: Steel with {c}% C: mass fraction of proeutectoid cementite by the lever rule {p}%
atlas_shade: Why it looks light or dark
atlas_forms: How it forms (alloy and heat treatment)
atlas_confuse: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
atlas_link_grain: Copy link to this grain size
atlas_grain_h: Grain size (grain size number and mean grain size)
atlas_grain_cmp: The idea of the comparison method
atlas_grain_cmp_lead: Grains one number apart, drawn at the same magnification. In the comparison method you match the specimen against standard charts like these.
atlas_g_cap: Schematic. Approx. magnification ×{m} (field width {w}), the equivalent of {n} grains in the field area
atlas_g_d: Mean grain diameter (square root of mean area)
atlas_g_n100: Grains per square inch at 100× (ASTM N)
atlas_g_count: Count the grains in the drawing
atlas_g_jeff: Planimetric: {i} grains inside + {c} grains cut by the frame × 1/2 + 1 for the corners = {n}. Divided by the field area {a} mm² gives {na} grains/mm² → G = {g}
atlas_g_icpt: Intercept: total test line length (dashed) {L} mm with {p} grain boundary intersections → ℓ̄ = {l} mm → G = {g}
atlas_g_count_note: The drawing uses {na} grains per mm² (the equivalent of {n} grains in the field area), and the grains continue beyond the frame. The counts give slightly different numbers because only a limited number of grains is counted and because of the grain shapes (see the note below).
atlas_practice_lead: Look at the schematic and choose the microstructure. After you answer you get the identification clues and how to tell it from the one you chose. The drawing changes a little every time.
atlas_p_shared: This question came from a shared link. This answer is not added to your record.
atlas_p_nostore: This browser cannot save the record; it will be lost when you close the page.
atlas_url_note: Your record stays in this browser and is never sent anywhere. A link copied before answering lets the recipient solve the same drawing; a link copied after answering opens your choice and the result.
home_feat_drill_desc: Practice calculation problems with new numbers every time, with worked steps
about_drill: practice standard materials science calculations, such as interplanar spacing, the lever rule, diffusion, fracture toughness and thermal stress, with new numbers each time. Answers are marked with units, with worked steps and the common mistake your number points to.
drill_noscript: Generating and marking problems needs JavaScript. You can still read the list of problem types and the notes on solving, units and significant figures below.
drill_answer_in: Give about {sig} significant figures. Tolerance ±{tol} %. Forms such as 2.3e-5 and 2.3×10^-5 are accepted.
drill_bad_input: That is not a number I can read. Examples: 0.287, 2.3e-5, 2.3×10^-5
drill_bad_unit: Unknown unit “{u}”. Choose the unit from the menu.
drill_h_sign: The sign is reversed. Check tension versus compression, or increase versus decrease.
drill_h_unit: This looks like a unit mix-up: your number is the value in {u}. In {uu} it is {a}.
drill_h_pow: You are off by a factor of 10^{n}. Check unit conversions (mm and m, kJ and J, cm³ and m³ and so on).
drill_h_close: Close, but outside the ±{tol} % tolerance. You may have rounded intermediate values too much or used a different constant from the problem.
drill_h_either: This value matches more than one common mistake (any of these is possible):
drill_tool_lead: Check it in the calculator, filled in with the same numbers:
drill_url_note: The URL holds only the problem type and a seed (?t=…&s=…), never the answer. Your record is saved only in this browser.
drill_sum_again: Another set with the same settings
drill_rec_empty: No record yet. Results are saved only in this browser.
drill_rec_clear_q: Clear the calculation drill record saved in this browser?
drill_types_lead: Click a type to get one problem of that type. Click a field name to start with that field selected.
home_feat_materials_desc: Find, compare and export property values with sources
about_materials: look up density, Young’s modulus, strength, thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, melting point, lattice constants and more for metals, ceramics, polymers, composite fibers and semiconductors, each value with its source and conditions. Switch units, compare 2–4 materials side by side and export CSV with a source column.
md_noscript: Search, filters, unit switching, comparison and CSV need JavaScript. The table below lists the main properties in the default units.
md_static_note: With JavaScript you can search, filter, sort and switch units in this table.
md_share_note: The URL keeps the search, filters, columns, units, sort, compared materials and the open card.
md_empty: No material matches. Shorten the search or reset the filters.
md_table_lead: Superscript numbers are source numbers (see the source list below); small text gives the grade, state, kind of strength and condition. “+n” is the number of other values for the same property: click the material name to see all of them on its card. Ranges show “low–high” and the representative value. Click a column heading to sort.
md_open_tool_note: Opens the calculator with this material’s values filled in.
md_cmp_lead: Materials ticked in the left column of the table (2–4) are lined up property by property.
md_cmp_empty: No material selected yet. Tick the left column of the table or use “Add to comparison” on a card.
md_cmp_one: {m} selected. Select at least one more to compare.
md_cmp_lead2: Ratios (×) take the first material ({m}) as 1. Ranges are compared by their representative values. Each material is compared by the first value shown in the table.
md_cmp_kind: Different kinds of strength ({l}). Compare ratios only between the same kind.
md_cmp_range: A range’s representative value is compared with a single value.
md_cmp_kelvin: Temperature ratios are calculated in kelvin.
md_cmp_nobase: The first material has no value here, so no ratio is shown.
md_cmp_max: You can compare up to 4 materials.
md_csv_wide: As in the table (one material per row; value, range, condition and source per column)
md_csv_long: All values (one value per row, with the value in its original unit)
md_csv_note: Exports the filtered materials in the displayed units (numbers keep the significant figures of the original values). The source column gives the name of each source.
md_chart_lead: The filtered materials, in descending order of the chosen property (up to 40). Lines are ranges; dots are representative or single values. Click a bar to open the material’s card.
md_chart_none: None of the filtered materials has a value for this property.
md_sources_lead: Numbers match the source numbers in the table and on the cards. Parentheses name the calculator that uses the values.
home_feat_formulas_desc: {n} materials science formulas with symbols, units, conditions and examples. Print only the ones you pick
about_formulas: materials science formulas with symbols and SI units, conditions of use, common mistakes and a numerical example, with the dimensions of every formula checked by machine. Print the formulas you pick as an A4 sheet, or share them as a link.
formulas_noscript: Search, filtering, picking and printing need JavaScript. All formulas are listed on this page.
formulas_search_ph: Name, symbol or term (e.g. Bragg, K_IC, diffusion length)
formulas_none: No formula matches. Try a shorter word or set the topic to “All”.
formulas_pick_first: Tick “Pick” on the formulas you want to print first.
formulas_sel_note: Your picks are kept in this browser only and never sent to a server.
formulas_dim_ok: both sides agree on every line ([ ] in SI base units)
